pharm: Synthetic nitrofuran applied topically; reductively activated by bacterial enzymes to reactive intermediates that inhibit bacterial carbohydrate metabolism, giving broad-spectrum bactericidal activity at the wound surface.
quick: Use only if benefit justifies risk
Caution with large/damaged areas (PEG base can accumulate)
summary: Nitrofurazone (nitrofural) is a topical nitrofuran antibacterial used as an adjunctive treatment for second- and third-degree burns (especially when resistance to other agents is a concern) and to prepare skin-graft surfaces. It is applied as a 0.2% cream, ointment, or soluble dressing. It is no longer FDA-approved as a marketed human product in the US (historic Furacin); the data here are drawn from older labels and regional sources. It is a notable contact sensitizer and animal studies showed carcinogenicity.
indications: Adjunctive antibacterial treatment of second- and third-degree burns, especially when bacterial resistance to other agents is a concern
Preparation of clean granulating skin surfaces for skin grafting
Surface bacterial infection of wounds, burns, and skin ulcers

dosage.t: Once daily or every few days per dressing technique
dosage.n: Reserve especially for resistance to other agents

dosage.t: Keep in contact at least 24 h; change several times daily or leave longer

admin: Apply directly to the lesion with a sterile spatula or place on sterile gauze laid against the wound; a bandage is optional
Flush residual product from the wound with sterile saline or water at dressing changes
Wear gloves and wash hands after applying (risk of sensitization in the applier)
Reassess the wound at about 3 days
moa: Bacterial nitroreductases reduce nitrofurazone to reactive intermediates that inhibit multiple bacterial enzymes involved in aerobic and anaerobic carbohydrate (glucose/pyruvate) metabolism and damage bacterial macromolecules including DNA, producing broad-spectrum bactericidal activity. The precise molecular mechanism is not fully understood.

absolute: Hypersensitivity to nitrofurazone or other nitrofurans or to excipients
relative: Renal dysfunction with extensive burns or large damaged areas (the polyethylene-glycol base can be absorbed and accumulate)
G6PD deficiency (risk of hemolysis, mainly with systemic exposure)

preg: Use only if the potential benefit justifies the potential risk; limited first-trimester topical data did not show an increase in defects.
lact: It is not known whether nitrofurazone is excreted in human milk; use only if clearly needed.
renal: Use with caution in renal impairment when applied to damaged skin or large areas, because the macrogol (polyethylene-glycol) base is absorbed through damaged skin and excreted unchanged by the kidney and can accumulate; avoid large-area use in significant chronic kidney disease or extensive burns.
hepatic: No specific dose adjustment; systemic absorption through intact skin is negligible.

common: Contact dermatitis and local skin reactions
serious: Renal effects from macrogol absorption in at-risk patients
rare: Carcinogenicity - demonstrated in animals only (IARC Group 3, not classifiable for humans)

monitoring: Local wound response (reassess at about 3 days)
Signs of sensitization or contact dermatitis
Renal function with large-area or damaged-skin use
Signs of superinfection with prolonged courses
counsel: For external use only; apply a thin layer to the area or onto gauze
Wear gloves and wash your hands after applying
Stop and seek advice if you develop a rash, redness, itching, or swelling, or if there is no improvement in about 3 days
Tell your clinician if you have G6PD deficiency, kidney problems, or extensive wounds
Inform your clinician if you are pregnant or breastfeeding; do not use longer than directed (risk of superinfection)
pk: Local antibacterial effect at the application site
Not applicable (negligible systemic absorption through intact skin)
Per dressing interval (kept in contact at least 24 h)
Protect from light; verify product-specific storage on the label
pearls: Not FDA-approved as a current marketed human product in the US - data here are from older labels and regional sources
An adjunctive/alternative agent, useful when wounds are resistant to other topicals and for graft-bed preparation
Broad Gram-positive and Gram-negative coverage and active in pus/blood, but may select for Pseudomonas
The polyethylene-glycol soluble-dressing base allows easy saline removal but is the basis for the renal caution
A notable contact allergen; animal carcinogenicity and sensitization drove withdrawal of US human products
missed: Apply the missed dressing when remembered; if it is near the next scheduled change, skip it - do not double up. There is no systemic risk.
overdose: Topical overdose is unlikely to cause systemic effects because absorption through intact skin is negligible - remove excess product and flush with sterile saline or water. With large damaged-skin areas, monitor for macrogol-related renal effects. Ingestion may cause GI upset and, in G6PD deficiency, hemolysis; management is supportive (no specific antidote).
